Below we compare “sport man” (fitness/recreational cycling prioritized riders) with “way of moving man” (mobility/convenience prioritized riders), focusing on cycling activities and purchase behavior. We draw on transport, consumer/marketing, and econometric evidence, with attention to gendered patterns and male-dominated subgroups.

Definitions and constructs
- Sport man: typically younger men who treat commuting and leisure riding as opportunities for fitness and performance, attracted to sporty/competitive bikes and upgrades, and sensitive to perceived effort and equipment quality. <cite id="05775974-0">Long-distance regular-bike commuters and speed pedelec users are more likely to be men, and younger people tend to commute more often by regular bike, with e-bikes and speed pedelecs broadening participation across profiles</cite>. 
- Way-of-moving man: typically convenience/time/cost/safety-oriented (often car or public transit users), prioritizing ease, reliability, and low friction; for those who do cycle, commuting is about utility, and barriers are infrastructure quality and weather. <cite id="05775974-1">In car‑dependent contexts, women (and those with caregiving chaining needs) report safety, comfort, and accessibility as more important than men’s, offering a lens on convenience/safety constraints that deter transport cycling</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Across populations, the top barriers to cycling are poor infrastructure (46%), feeling unsafe (40%), and bad weather (34%), while time saving ranks highly among travel benefits</cite>.

Cycling activities: frequency, intensity, and purposes
- Sport man’s activity profile: distance, intensity, and sportification. <cite id="05775974-0">Men are more likely than women among long‑distance regular‑bike commuters, and speed pedelec users are more likely to be men</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Physical fitness is the most commonly mentioned motive for purchasing a bicycle or e‑bike, and bicycle riders replace urban transport to work more than e‑bikers, indicating a stronger substitution of commuting for fitness‑oriented riding</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Compared with e‑bike respondents, regular‑bike respondents have more mountain and racing/road styles, reflecting sport/competitive orientation</cite>. 
- Way‑of‑moving man’s activity profile: utility‑driven, shorter to medium trips, and sensitive to comfort/safety and time. <cite id="05775974-1">Long average commute trip lengths (10–15 km in Australian cities) appeal to fit and motivated riders, but discourage others; women and caregivers disproportionately face safety, comfort, accessibility, and trip‑chaining constraints</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Saving time ranks high in travel choice benefits, while comfort and fitness are split—underscoring that convenience-oriented riders care more about speed/effort minimization than sport-oriented riders</cite>. 
- Cross-cutting barrier differences. <cite id="cbc13836-2">The largest barriers are infrastructure quality/safety and weather</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">In Norway’s low‑cycling context, “lycra‑cyclists” (training‑oriented, highly equipped, often men) value exercise above all; an e‑bike can be counter‑motivational for this subgroup, though WTP for bikes and accessories is high</cite>. <cite id="05775974-1">Women report safety concerns more often, suggesting that improving comfort, security, and accessibility can convert mobility‑oriented users</cite>.

Purchase behavior: what they buy and how they decide
- Motives and product mix. <cite id="cbc13836-0">E‑bike buyers skew to city/commuter models, whereas bicycle owners have more mountain and racing/road bikes; e‑bike users ride more frequently</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Physical fitness is the top motive for purchasing a bike or e‑bike; in the e‑bike group, convenience (ease of cycling) is twice as often cited as in the bicycle group; environment or cost savings play minor roles</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">Those who want to drive less show interest in e‑bikes, while those already cycling much are less interested; WTP for an e‑bike is nuanced: people willing to pay much for an ordinary bike are willing to pay more for an e‑bike, but “lycra‑cyclists” (often men) may reject e‑bikes because they run counter to exercise motivations</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Millennials/Gen X e‑bike motives include time‑saving and environmental improvement rather than “just to keep healthy,” implying different purchase levers</cite>.
- Willingness to pay for bikes and infrastructure. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Only 6% “absolutely” and 23% “yes probably” consider buying an e‑bike today; interest peaks among those cycling up to 10 km/week and falls among heavy cyclists (>20 km/week)</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">WTP to pay extra for an e‑bike and WTP for an e‑bike overall increased after awareness interventions for those willing to drive less; baseline WTP to pay extra for an e‑bike was 10.14 NOK (test) vs 8.60 NOK (control), and total WTP 388 NOK vs 303 NOK, indicating responsiveness to framing and needs</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Saving time ranks highest in travel benefits (average score 5.8), implying mobility‑oriented men are more receptive to offers that reduce cycling effort/time (e.g., cargo bikes with child‑carrying accessories, secure locks, weather protection) than to purely fitness messaging</cite>.
- Substitution and replacement of car use. <cite id="5d126fae-0">E‑bikers replace cars more than bicycle riders, while bicycle riders replace urban transport to work more than e‑bikers; motives differ, with fitness salient for bike purchase and convenience salient for e‑bike</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Commuter e‑bikes dominate e‑bike ownership, suggesting that mobility‑oriented men adopt e‑bikes for “last‑mile” convenience and reliability</cite>.
- Non-monetary levers (comfort, safety, convenience). <cite id="05775974-1">Gendered travel constraints—safety, comfort, accessibility, and trip chaining—suggest that mobility‑oriented men value reliable, secure, and multifunctional bikes (e.g., cargo or hybrid, lights, locks, racks), while sport‑oriented men prioritize performance and aesthetics</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Perceived safety and infrastructure quality are the top barriers; thus, signaling safety (reflectors, lights, bells) and urban‑ready comfort (sealed saddles, upright geometry, fenders) can move convenience‑oriented buyers</cite>.

Interactions: mode choice, activities, and purchases
- Fitness and commuting entanglement. <cite id="05775974-1">Long commute distances can transform the commute into a fitness opportunity for sporty riders, attracting younger, male, fit riders</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Bicycle owners replace more car trips for commuting than e‑bikers, consistent with sporty riders substituting car trips when fitness is a primary motive</cite>.
- Effort/time and infrastructure as switching costs. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Saving time ranks high in travel benefits, but comfort and fitness are split; the largest barriers are infrastructure quality/safety and weather</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">For mobility‑oriented men, improving infrastructure and reducing perceived effort (e.g., e‑cargo/hybrid options) increases WTP to switch from cars, though some “lycra‑cyclists” resist e‑bikes</cite>.
- Product implications. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Sports‑oriented consumers skew to racing/road and mountain styles and likely invest in performance gear/upgrades; commuter e‑bikes dominate among e‑bike buyers</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Fitness and convenience are the two strongest purchase motives, with environment/cost minor; thus, marketing to sport men should emphasize performance, durability, and community, while mobility men respond to time/cost savings, reliability, and risk reduction</cite>.

Segments and demographics
- Men in both groups. <cite id="05775974-0">Men are more likely than women to be long‑distance regular‑bike commuters and speed pedelec users</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">“Lycra‑cyclists” are often men and highly WTP for sports equipment; e‑bikes can conflict with exercise motives</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Millennials/Gen X e‑bike buyers value time and environment more than health, favoring commuter models</cite>. <cite id="05775974-2">Event‑recruited U.S. cyclist samples are 70.8% male and report high confidence, suggesting experienced sport/recreational overlap</cite>.
- Mobility‑oriented car commuters. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Saving time is the top travel benefit; infrastructure quality/safety and weather are top barriers</cite>. <cite id="05775974-1">Women and caregivers disproportionately cite safety, comfort, accessibility, and trip‑chaining constraints, indicating that mobility‑oriented men—who value efficiency—may be swayed by convenience plus reliability/safety assurances</cite>.

Interventions and nudges that change both activity and purchases
- Education and WTP for e‑bikes and infrastructure. <cite id="cbc13836-1">An intervention increased WTP to pay extra for an e‑bike and total WTP for an e‑bike among those willing to drive less; people willing to pay much for ordinary bikes also showed higher WTP for e‑bikes, indicating that education can convert mobility‑oriented demand and that existing cycling investment can move price‑sensitive segments</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Awareness of barriers and benefits shifts stated interest in e‑bikes by weekly cycling distance, with highest interest among light riders and lowest among heavy riders</cite>.
- Commuting substitution and health messaging. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Bicycle purchase for commuting substitutes car trips more than e‑bike purchase, while fitness is the dominant purchase motive; thus, bike-to-work schemes and fitness messaging can increase both cycling activity and purchases</cite>.
- Safety/comfort upgrades for conversion. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Improving infrastructure and offering accessories that reduce perceived effort/safety risk (lights, reflectors, sealed saddles, fenders, locks) can lower barriers for mobility‑oriented men, moving them from car to bike</cite>. <cite id="05775974-1">Trip-chaining needs and childcare suggest demand for cargo/pedal trailers and secure racks, aligning purchases with daily mobility</cite>.

Practical implications for marketing and policy
- To sport man: emphasize performance, aesthetics, and fitness outcomes; offer racing/road and mountain styles, performance tires/wheels, power meters, and safety gear as status/performance signals. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Competitive styles dominate among bicycle owners</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Fitness is the top purchase motive</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">Lycra‑cyclists are often men with high WTP for sports equipment</cite>.
- To way‑of‑moving man: emphasize time/cost savings, reliability, and risk reduction; prioritize commuter/e‑bike models, cargo hybrids, and accessories that make cycling as effortless as driving. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Saving time is the top benefit; infrastructure/safety and weather are top barriers</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Commuter e‑bikes dominate e‑bike ownership</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">Education and WTP nudges increase e‑bike uptake among car‑oriented segments</cite>.
- Cross-cutting: invest in safe, connected cycling networks and integrate point‑of‑sale bundles (lights, locks, racks, fenders) with clear time/cost savings messaging to reduce switching costs. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Poor infrastructure/safety and weather depress activity; time savings are salient for travel choice</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Bike purchase substitutes commuting car trips more than e‑bike purchase</cite>.

Limitations and evidence gaps
- Direct segmentation of “mobility‑oriented men” by brand preference and price sensitivity is thin in open‑population studies; most evidence aggregates men or contrasts cyclists vs non‑cyclists. <cite id="cbc13836-0">Survey samples skew to higher‑income, experienced riders</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Self‑selection and coverage limits (e.g., e‑commerce markets) reduce representativeness</cite>. 
- What would resolve gaps: representative national panels with cluster analysis on male subsegments (fitness‑oriented vs convenience‑oriented), measuring brand loyalty, price elasticity across bike types, and WTP to pay for infrastructure vs equipment; causal field experiments (bike-to-work subsidies, accessory bundles, network improvements) with purchase and usage outcomes by segment.

Summary comparison
- Activities: Sport man cycles more for fitness and sport, often commuting long distances using the ride as training; way‑of‑moving man cycles for utility, seeking low effort/time and reliability. <cite id="05775974-0">Men dominate long‑distance regular‑bike and speed pedelec commuting</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Fitness is the top purchase motive; bicycle riders replace more car commuting than e‑bikers</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Saving time ranks highest among travel benefits, while safety/infrastructure and weather are top barriers</cite>.
- Purchases: Sport man favors performance‑oriented bikes and invests in upgrades and safety gear aligned with training/riding identity. <cite id="cbc13836-0">More mountain/road styles among bicycle owners</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">High WTP for sports equipment among lycra‑cyclists (often men)</cite>. Way‑of‑moving man favors commuter/e‑bikes and multifunctional accessories that reduce effort/time and risk. <cite id="cbc13836-0">E‑bike models are predominantly commuter</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Convenience is twice as often a motive among e‑bike buyers; fitness dominates overall but environment/cost are minor</cite>. Education and infrastructure improvements shift both activity and purchase interest. <cite id="cbc13836-1">WTP for e‑bikes rises after interventions targeting car reduction; heavy cyclists show lower interest in e‑bikes</cite>.
- Policy/marketing: For sport man, performance and community; for way‑of‑moving man, time/cost savings, safety, and convenience. <cite id="cbc13836-2">Network quality and weather sensitivity are major constraints to overcome</cite>. <cite id="5d126fae-0">Bike‑to‑work schemes and fitness messaging increase commuting substitution</cite>. <cite id="cbc13836-1">E‑bike and accessory bundling can convert mobility‑oriented users when effort/time barriers are addressed</cite>.

Title: Gender differences in recreational and transport cycling: a cross-sectional mixed-methods comparison of cycling patterns, motivators, and constraints
Snippet: Gender differences in transport cycling in Australia and other car-dependent countries reflect in part the different transportation patterns, needs, and purposes of men and women [12,13]. For example, issues of safety, comfort and accessibility to destinations appear to be more important to women's overall travel behavior than to men's [14]. This may partly explain the low transport cycling rates for women, as studies have found that women are more likely than men to report safety concerns as constraining their transport cycling [15]. Gender differences may also be explained by the nature of a typical transport cycling journey in Australia. The average cycle commute trip length is high, 10 km in Queensland [9] and 11-15 km in Melbourne [15], generally higher than seen in Europe [16]. Such trips may appeal to the most motivated, fit and sporty recreational cyclists, as the commute to work becomes an opportunity to improve fitness; however, the long distances may discourage other cyclists and women disproportionately so. International data indicate that women are more likely than men to trip chain as part of their commute, given their responsibilities for transporting children and other household members and to do the household shopping [12]. These tasks require different cycling equipment and cycling style to those which are common in countries such as Australia [10]. 

Although gender differences are noted in travel patterns in general and in transport cycling specifically, studies have tended to make broad comparisons, and few studies have focused on modeling male and female cycling patterns separately [13,17]. Given the low prevalence of transport cycling in countries like Australia, this modeling is difficult to achieve in studies of the general population as so few people report cycling. Studies which explicitly sample cyclists can provide valuable data on gender differences in cycling behavior. The primary aims of this study were to examine, in a population of current cyclists, gender differences in cycling patterns and in motivators and barriers to cycling, separately for recreational and transport cycling. A secondary aim was to explore possible overlaps in cycling patterns between recreational and transport cycling to better understand gender differences in cycling for different purposes. Most of the data collected to address our aims were quantitative; however, some qualitative data were gathered to expand the knowledge obtained from the quantitative findings.

Title: Differences of Cycling Experiences and Perceptions between E-Bike and Bicycle Users in the United States
Snippet: The purpose of this paper was to study the differences of cycling experience and perception of e-bike and bicycle users, and factors influencing the e-bike purchase decisions of bicycle users. Our study builds on previous studies exploring e-bike cycling experience and perception. However, this study focused on a comparison of differences of cycling experiences and perceptions between e-bike and bicycle users in the United States, where e-bikes are a new transportation mode. The e-bike market has matured since previous studies. Purpose-built e-bikes capture a large market share, in contrast with about half of the respondents converting conventional bicycles to e-bikes in MacArthur's study in 2013, the first nationwide survey of e-bike users in North America [1]. Also, our study is the first in the U.S. to evaluate e-bike purchase intention potential using multivariate modelling approaches. While several studies have focused on the role of an e-bike to assist older people to overcome riding barriers and to use for recreational purposes, we found that Millennials and Generation X respondents have some different e-bike cycling motives, such as cycling to save time and improve the environment, rather just to keep healthy [1,14]. Several studies reveal that e-bikes have increased riding rates and distance traveled, supporting our findings [1,12,15]. 

The data was from a U.S.-based end-consumer online survey that was distributed via IBDs. The e-bike models were predominately city/commuter (33% of EO, 31% of BE) with other commuter and on-road styles, whereas the conventional models varied, having higher numbers of more competitive styles, such as mountain and racing/road. E-bike respondents use their e-bikes more frequently than conventional bicyclists.

Title: Differences of Cycling Experiences and Perceptions between E-Bike and Bicycle Users in the United States
Snippet: The purpose of this paper was to study the differences of cycling experience and perception of e-bike and bicycle users, and factors influencing the e-bike purchase decisions of bicycle users. Our study builds on previous studies exploring e-bike cycling experience and perception. However, this study focused on a comparison of differences of cycling experiences and perceptions between e-bike and bicycle users in the United States, where e-bikes are a new transportation mode. The e-bike market has matured since previous studies. Purpose-built e-bikes capture a large market share, in contrast with about half of the respondents converting conventional bicycles to e-bikes in MacArthur's study in 2013, the first nationwide survey of e-bike users in North America [1]. Also, our study is the first in the U.S. to evaluate e-bike purchase intention potential using multivariate modelling approaches. While several studies have focused on the role of an e-bike to assist older people to overcome riding barriers and to use for recreational purposes, we found that Millennials and Generation X respondents have some different e-bike cycling motives, such as cycling to save time and improve the environment, rather just to keep healthy [1,14]. Several studies reveal that e-bikes have increased riding rates and distance traveled, supporting our findings [1,12,15]. 

The data was from a U.S.-based end-consumer online survey that was distributed via IBDs. A total of 806 respondents in the U.S. took the completed survey, in which 387 respondents own regular bicycles, 122 respondents only own e-bikes, and 241 respondents own both bicycles and e-bikes. E-bike and bicycle respondents have similar demographic characteristics, including education level, household income, and family structure. The cycling characteristics and behaviors of bicycle and e-bike users were also compared and analyzed. The e-bike models were predominately city/commuter (33% of EO, 31% of BE) with other commuter and on-road styles, whereas the conventional models varied, having higher numbers of more competitive styles, such as mountain and racing/road. Title: Bicycle commuting beyond short distances: built environment, socio-demographic factors and type of bicycle influencing the choice to cycle to three university campuses.
Snippet: Witlox and Tindemans ( 2004) suggested that in the urban region of Ghent (Belgium), cycle commuters are more likely to be women. This differs from the findings of our data, where men, especially those living in dense and mixed-land use areas, are more likely to commute by regular bicycle regardless of the distance cycled. Our study confirms the results of the few identified empirical studies on long-distance cyclists (Hansen & Nielsen, 2014;Manaugh et al., 2017;Nordengen et al., 2019) that these are more likely to be men. However, cyclists commuting longer distances by e-bikes are more likely to be older and female. In contrast, Speedpedelec users are more likely to be men, confirming the results of van der Salm et al. (2022). Furthermore, our findings are in line with previous research carried out by Vandenbulcke et al. (2011), who concluded that younger people tend to commute more often by regular bike. Moreover, our study adds to the existing literature that age has no effect on the choice to commute by an e-bike regardless of the distance cycled and reveals that e-bikes and speedpedelecs broaden participation in cycling across various socio-demographic profiles in combination with certain built environment characteristics.

Title: Gender differences in recreational and transport cycling: a cross-sectional mixed-methods comparison of cycling patterns, motivators, and constraints
Snippet: Gender differences in transport cycling in Australia and other car-dependent countries reflect in part the different transportation patterns, needs, and purposes of men and women [12,13]. For example, issues of safety, comfort and accessibility to destinations appear to be more important to women's overall travel behavior than to men's [14]. This may partly explain the low transport cycling rates for women, as studies have found that women are more likely than men to report safety concerns as constraining their transport cycling [15]. Gender differences may also be explained by the nature of a typical transport cycling journey in Australia. The average cycle commute trip length is high, 10 km in Queensland [9] and 11-15 km in Melbourne [15], generally higher than seen in Europe [16]. Such trips may appeal to the most motivated, fit and sporty recreational cyclists, as the commute to work becomes an opportunity to improve fitness; however, the long distances may discourage other cyclists and women disproportionately so. International data indicate that women are more likely than men to trip chain as part of their commute, given their responsibilities for transporting children and other household members and to do the household shopping [12]. These tasks require different cycling equipment and cycling style to those which are common in countries such as Australia [10]. 

Although gender differences are noted in travel patterns in general and in transport cycling specifically, studies have tended to make broad comparisons, and few studies have focused on modeling male and female cycling patterns separately [13,17]. Given the low prevalence of transport cycling in countries like Australia, this modeling is difficult to achieve in studies of the general population as so few people report cycling. Studies which explicitly sample cyclists can provide valuable data on gender differences in cycling behavior. The primary aims of this study were to examine, in a population of current cyclists, gender differences in cycling patterns and in motivators and barriers to cycling, separately for recreational and transport cycling. A secondary aim was to explore possible overlaps in cycling patterns between recreational and transport cycling to better understand gender differences in cycling for different purposes. Most of the data collected to address our aims were quantitative; however, some qualitative data were gathered to expand the knowledge obtained from the quantitative findings.

Title: Assessing the Bicycle Network in St. Louis: A PlaceBased User-Centered Approach
Snippet: Surveys were distributed by two methods for six weeks from August to September of 2015. We established booths at four local cycling events hosted by Saint Louis University and Trailnet, a local bicycle advocacy organization. Participants were recruited to voluntarily complete the survey in person and on site. Persons over the age of 18 who had recently ridden a bicycle on the streets within the study area were allowed to participate in the survey. The study did not differentiate between bicycle commuters and recreational cyclists, as both are considered users of the bicycle network and are equally affected by the environmental variables along their routes. 

In total, 89 surveys were completed and used in the study. Sixty-three participants were male, representing 70.8% of the total (Table 1). While inconsistent with the total population of adult bike riders in the U.S., which is 54% male [55], the sample is consistent with the percentage of male cyclists found in a previous St. Louis study [57] as well as in national bike commuting statistics [58]. Most participants, 49 (55%), responded that they were very confident, while 37 (41.6%) were confident. This was expected, as most participants were recruited at bicycling events. Results therefore will reflect the opinions of very confident or confident cyclists. This reported cycling confidence suggests that participants were likely experienced cyclists, capable of providing accurate assessments of their routes.

documents.title: Gender differences in recreational and transport cycling: a cross-sectional mixed-methods comparison of cycling patterns, motivators, and constraints
documents.snippet:
Gender differences in transport cycling in Australia and other car-dependent countries reflect in part the different transportation patterns, needs, and purposes of men and women [12,13]. For example, issues of safety, comfort and accessibility to destinations appear to be more important to women's overall travel behavior than to men's [14]. This may partly explain the low transport cycling rates for women, as studies have found that women are more likely than men to report safety concerns as constraining their transport cycling [15]. Gender differences may also be explained by the nature of a typical transport cycling journey in Australia. The average cycle commute trip length is high, 10 km in Queensland [9] and 11-15 km in Melbourne [15], generally higher than seen in Europe [16]. Such trips may appeal to the most motivated, fit and sporty recreational cyclists, as the commute to work becomes an opportunity to improve fitness; however, the long distances may discourage other cyclists and women disproportionately so. International data indicate that women are more likely than men to trip chain as part of their commute, given their responsibilities for transporting children and other household members and to do the household shopping [12]. These tasks require different cycling equipment and cycling style to those which are common in countries such as Australia [10]. 

Although gender differences are noted in travel patterns in general and in transport cycling specifically, studies have tended to make broad comparisons, and few studies have focused on modeling male and female cycling patterns separately [13,17]. Given the low prevalence of transport cycling in countries like Australia, this modeling is difficult to achieve in studies of the general population as so few people report cycling. Studies which explicitly sample cyclists can provide valuable data on gender differences in cycling behavior. The primary aims of this study were to examine, in a population of current cyclists, gender differences in cycling patterns and in motivators and barriers to cycling, separately for recreational and transport cycling. A secondary aim was to explore possible overlaps in cycling patterns between recreational and transport cycling to better understand gender differences in cycling for different purposes. Most of the data collected to address our aims were quantitative; however, some qualitative data were gathered to expand the knowledge obtained from the quantitative findings.

Title: Differences of Cycling Experiences and Perceptions between E-Bike and Bicycle Users in the United States
Snippet: An online survey was conducted by Bosch eBike Systems from September 2015 to October 2015. The survey was an end-consumer online survey in the United States, which was distributed via IBDs. This survey intended to explore customers' perception of e-bikes and conventional bicycles, attempted to reveal bicycle users' riding habits, and estimated the potential opportunities and barriers to e-bike purchase. The survey questions were developed following an e-bike literature review related to e-bike purchase and riding behavior [1,6,12]. This survey focused on fully assembled e-bikes (e-bike conversions from a standard bicycle were excluded). The entire survey covers four aspects of e-bike and bicycle owners, including household characteristics, cycling experiences and behavior, motives and perception for e-bike use, future e-bike expectation, and purchase interest (for conventional bicycle owners only). Respondents who owned both a bicycle and an e-bike were presented with the e-bike related questionnaire. As an incentive for participation, respondents were entered into a chance to win an e-bike. Table 1 presents an overview summary of the survey scope. The authors acknowledge the limitations of relying solely on this sub-sample, likely missing a large portion of the e-bike market, particularly those purchased online or from big-box stores. As with most survey research, our study could suffer from self-selection bias. However, we think that this sample still represents a large and growing proportion of the current and future bicycle and e-bike markets, by both volume and value. Thus, the insights gained could provide value to public and private sector decision-makers regarding future e-bike ownership and use. 

A total of 806 respondents in the U.S. completed the survey. In the survey, 56 respondents claimed that they did not have a bicycle or e-bike. Of those, 47% said that they lived in an area which is not safe to ride, or is too hilly, or that has poor bicycling infrastructure. In addition, 15% of these respondents cannot ride because of physical limitations. Also, there were 15 bicycle respondents which stated that they no longer ride their bicycle because of physical limitations and/or because the area they live in is too hilly. These 56 respondents were excluded from the following analysis. So, the final total sample is 750 respondents.

This survey intended to explore customers' perception of e-bikes and conventional bicycles, attempted to reveal bicycle users' riding habits, and estimated the potential opportunities and barriers to e-bike purchase. The survey questions were developed following an e-bike literature review related to e-bike purchase and riding behavior [1,6,12]. This survey focused on fully assembled e-bikes (e-bike conversions from a standard bicycle were excluded). Respondents who owned both a bicycle and an e-bike were presented with the e-bike related questionnaire. As an incentive for participation, respondents were entered into a chance to win an e-bike. Table 1 presents an overview summary of the survey scope. The authors acknowledge the limitations of relying solely on this sub-sample, likely missing a large portion of the e-bike market, particularly those purchased online or from big-box stores. As with most survey research, our study could suffer from self-selection bias. However, we think that this sample still represents a large and growing proportion of the current and future bicycle and e-bike markets, by both volume and value. Thus, the insights gained could provide value to public and private sector decision-makers regarding future e-bike ownership and use. 

A total of 806 respondents in the U.S. completed the survey. In the survey, 56 respondents claimed that they did not have a bicycle or e-bike. Of those, 47% said that they lived in an area which is not safe to ride, or is too hilly, or that has poor bicycling infrastructure. In addition, 15% of these respondents cannot ride because of physical limitations. Also, there were 15 bicycle respondents which stated that they no longer ride their bicycle because of physical limitations and/or because the area they live in is too hilly. These 56 respondents were excluded from the following analysis. So, the final total sample is 750 respondents.

# Summary Answer

Purchase sequences reveal escalation of commitment through patterns of sunk-costed early investments, ambiguous or reinforcing feedback, and social/structural norms that lock buyers into further purchases or upgrades. <cite id="fb02fcb8-0">Escalation arises when decision makers feel obliged to continue investing resources (money, time, effort) due to mechanisms such as justification/consistency pressures, perceived probabilities of future outcomes, and the value of sunk costs, making continuation look “rational” even as outcomes worsen</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-2">Determinants cluster into project-, psychological-, social-, and structural-level factors, and escalation is often diagnosed when consecutive gates or approvals occur without objective re-evaluation</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-4">Operationally, escalation looks like buying more while prior investments fail, with ambiguity in feedback and lack of objective criteria amplifying persistence</cite>.

For sport cyclists, purchase sequences tend to be identity-driven and social: acquiring road/mountain bikes, then sport-specific accessories (helmets, bar-end mirrors, bags), followed by training-oriented upgrades, with high investment and community norms sustaining persistence even when results plateau. <cite id="cd3543f7-0">Athletic identity is positively related to commitment to sport; the stronger one identifies with the athlete role, the more they invest time, money, and effort and the more they feel obligated to persist</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-2">Social cohesion on teams reinforces commitment and attendance, and athletic identity mediates between sport commitment and participation; commitment predicts behavioral persistence</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-3">Community narratives and team/athlete identification elevate pride and loyalty, shaping brand and behavioral commitments</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-1">Road cycling’s precarious employment structures and long racing seasons embed riders in small-knit groups and norms of intense season-long work, making loyalty to team/community feel obligatory and heightening persistence in the face of risk</cite>.

For transportation cyclists (commuter/cargo/e-bike), purchase sequences emphasize utility, safety, and convenience, moving through commuter bike/e-bike adoption, then essential accessories (helmets, lights, locks, bags), often with post-purchase mode shifts (replacing car trips), and with clearer instrumental feedback. <cite id="11d642de-0">Compared with conventional-bike users, e-bike users disproportionately own city/commuter-oriented bikes and report higher frequency of use, with different motives (time saving, environmental benefits) than road/mountain users</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-1">City/commuter bikes dominate among e-bike owners, while road bikes are far less represented, indicating different product ecosystems and usage contexts</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-2">Cargo-bike owners exhibit measurable travel-mode changes after purchase (e.g., substituting car trips), suggesting clear instrumental outcomes that can either reinforce or motivate de-escalation if goals are unmet</cite>. <cite id="f3989761-0">Ecommerce behavior around cycling shows sequential acquisition of safety/durability-oriented items (helmets, phone mounts, waterproof cases) and bags, with users progressing through information search, evaluation, purchase, and cross-sell opportunities</cite>. <cite id="f3989761-1">Purchase journeys can be modeled as phased funnels: need recognition, information search, alternative evaluation, purchase decision, consumption, postpurchase evaluation, and divestment</cite>.

Overall, sport cyclists show stronger social-psychological escalation cues (identity, team norms, visibility of participation), making it easier to escalate after early sunk-cost investments (bike + gear), whereas transportation cyclists are more sensitive to instrumental feedback and switching costs; their purchase sequences reveal escalation when commuting benefits materialize (time saved, reliability), and de-escalation when they fail to meet thresholds, with accessory additions serving as incremental commitments rather than identity-driven rites of passage. <cite id="fb02fcb8-2">Escalation risk increases when feedback is ambiguous and organizational/project norms discourage re-evaluation</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-4">Ambiguity and lack of objective criteria increase escalation; clarity in outcomes (e.g., minutes saved) can enable clearer de-escalation</cite>.

# Concepts: Commitment Escalation and Purchase Sequences

<cite id="fb02fcb8-0">Commitment escalation theory holds that decision makers justify prior investments through consistency and self-image, perceive changing probabilities as tipping in favor of continuing, and overweight the value of sunk costs, leading to continuation even when evidence warrants stoppage</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-1">In new product and cost-saving project settings, escalation is evident when the same gatekeeper approves two consecutive gates for a failing project, delaying stop decisions</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-2">Determinants cluster into project-, psychological-, social-, and structural-level factors, and escalation can be alleviated by structured de-escalation processes (e.g., phased reviews) or by reducing commitment through switching or reframing</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-3">De-escalation is the reduction or redirection of commitment to failing courses of action; research shows escalation cycles can be broken by considering alternatives and reducing commitment when feedback is negative</cite>. <cite id="fb02fcb8-4">Three escalation characteristics are: significant prior resource investment, negative feedback, and a choice to continue investing to share sunk losses; ambiguity and social norms exacerbate persistence</cite>.

Purchase sequences operationalize these mechanisms across stages: <cite id="f3989761-1">from need recognition and information search to purchase, consumption, and postpurchase evaluation, with multiple touchpoints and cross-sell opportunities shaping subsequent choices</cite>. <cite id="f3989761-0">User profiles and sequential purchase histories reveal progression toward complementary cycling gear (helmets, bags, mounts), signaling ecosystem lock-in and incremental commitment</cite>.

# How Sport vs Transportation Cyclists Differ in Purchase Sequences

Bike type and ecosystem:
- Sport cyclists prioritize road or mountain bikes and sport-specific gear; commuter and cargo bikes cluster in city/commuter categories. <cite id="11d642de-1">City/commuter bikes are the predominant e-bike type, while road bikes are far more common among bicycle owners than among e-bike owners</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-0">Compared with bicycle-only users, e-bike users more often cite time-saving and environmental motives and ride more frequently</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-2">Athletic identity mediates commitment and participation intensity, with social cohesion reinforcing attendance and persistence</cite>.

- Transportation cyclists emphasize utility, safety, and convenience, progressing through bike acquisition, then required accessories (helmet, lights/lock, bags), and possibly e-bike upgrades for reliability; post-purchase, they evaluate whether car trips are replaced. <cite id="f3989761-0">Sequential purchases of helmets, phone mounts, waterproof phone cases, and bags reflect a practical safety–convenience ecosystem</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-2">Cargo-bike buyers report changes in mode split after purchase, with stronger evidence of replacing auto trips than bicycle-only users</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-4">Gendered cargo-bike studies show behavioral shifts and qualitative insights into post-purchase use, highlighting utility as a driver</cite>.

Escalation signatures:
- Sport cyclists: <cite id="cd3543f7-0">Identity- and community-driven persistence</cite> and <cite id="cd3543f7-1">embedded norms of long racing seasons and team obligations</cite> can produce escalation even when results plateau; <cite id="cd3543f7-2">social cohesion and identity jointly predict ongoing investments and behavior</cite>. Purchase sequences include visible status cues (road bikes, premium helmets, bar-end mirrors) and continuous upgrades, with de-escalation harder when social narratives frame nonparticipation as loss of identity. <cite id="cd3543f7-3">Narratives of pride and community loyalty elevate commitment to teams/athletes and sustain consumer-athlete relationships</cite>.

- Transportation cyclists: <cite id="11d642de-0">Higher frequency of use and instrumental motives</cite> produce clearer feedback on utility; sequences reveal escalation when commuting time or reliability expectations are met, and de-escalation when not. <cite id="f3989761-1">Postpurchase evaluation and potential divestment are explicit phases</cite>, and accessory additions function as low-cost commitment tests (e.g., lights/lock/bags) rather than identity rites; failure to realize time savings can trigger exit or minimal upgrades. <cite id="11d642de-2">Cargo-bike users’ documented mode shifts illustrate successful escalation; lack of shift suggests de-escalation potential</cite>.

# Why Escalation Plays Out Differently

Mechanisms and context:
- Sunk costs and irreversibility: <cite id="fb02fcb8-0">Valuation of sunk costs increases escalation risk when early investments cannot be recovered or reframed</cite>; sport bikes and sport gear are often high-ticket and status-laden, whereas commuter bikes and accessories are modular, lowering irreversibility per dollar. <cite id="fb02fcb8-2">Structural gatekeeping and norms reduce re-evaluation; in sport communities, team/coach structures can act as “gates” discouraging exit</cite>.

- Feedback and ambiguity: <cite id="fb02fcb8-4">Ambiguous feedback amplifies escalation; objective criteria reduce it</cite>. Sport outcomes (fitness, speed) are inherently variable and socially comparative, sustaining commitment despite plateau; commuter outcomes (time saved, reliability) are quantifiable, enabling escalation when thresholds are met and de-escalation when not. <cite id="fb02fcb8-3">De-escalation strategies—early, low-cost course corrections or redirection—are more feasible in commuter ecosystems</cite>.

- Social identity and community: <cite id="cd3543f7-0">Athletic identity grows with time and financial/effort investment and increases commitment</cite>, while <cite id="cd3543f7-1">road cycling’s organizational structure and norms create precarious yet tightly knit communities that heighten loyalty pressures</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-2">Social cohesion on teams predicts attendance and behavioral commitment, reinforcing escalations</cite>. Conversely, commuter cyclists’ identities are less tied to visible peer groups and more to practical roles, making social disapproval of underuse less potent than in sport communities. <cite id="cd3543f7-3">Narratives linking athletes to place/community magnify loyalty and persistence</cite>.

- Ecosystem design and switching costs: <cite id="f3989761-0">Sequential purchases of complementary cycling gear raise switching costs and lock users into brand ecosystems</cite>, but commuter ecosystems typically allow easier substitution (e.g., another bike brand or transit). <cite id="f3989761-1">Phased funnels enable targeted interventions at information search or postpurchase evaluation to reduce overcommitment</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-1">Commuter-oriented bike dominance among e-bike owners indicates lower brand lock-in and higher modality flexibility</cite>.

# Evidence From Purchase Journeys and Postpurchase Outcomes

- E-bike vs conventional-bike users: <cite id="11d642de-0">E-bike users report more frequent cycling and different motives (time and environment) than conventional bicycle users, suggesting purchase sequences with stronger instrumental feedback loops</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-1">Commuter bike share among e-bike owners far exceeds road bike share, reflecting different accessory and upgrade paths (lights, locks, e-bike kits) than sport-oriented users</cite>.

- Cargo-bike adoption: <cite id="11d642de-2">Postpurchase surveys show mode substitution and usage patterns after purchase, validating the instrumental feedback crucial for escalation diagnosis</cite>.

- Consumer purchase journey structure: <cite id="f3989761-1">Standard funnel phases (need recognition, search, evaluation, purchase, consumption, postpurchase, divestment) govern cycling purchase sequences, with multiple touchpoints for reframing or exit</cite>. <cite id="f3989761-0">Accessories purchased after a base bike (helmets, phone mounts, waterproof cases, bags) indicate ecosystem progression and incremental commitment; user profiles show readiness for the next major purchase (e.g., a new helmet, bag, or bike)</cite>.

- Sport identity and persistence: <cite id="cd3543f7-0">Athletic identity increases with participation investments and predicts continued engagement</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-2">Social cohesion and identity jointly predict commitment and weekly participation; commitment then predicts behavioral persistence</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-3">Narratives of pride and community strengthen identification and loyalty</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-1">Normative workloads and team dependence in professional cycling illustrate structural pressures that heighten escalation risks</cite>.

# Managerial and Data Implications

- Diagnose escalation vs reallocated commitment: <cite id="fb02fcb8-1">Consecutive approvals without objective reassessment signal escalation</cite>. For sport brands, watch for repeated accessory upgrades and race registrations without performance gains; for commuter brands, monitor whether accessory additions yield expected time savings. <cite id="fb02fcb8-2">Structured de-escalation gates in the journey (e.g., mid-course reviews for accessory bundles) can curb escalation</cite>.

- Tailor journey design by segment:
  - Sport cyclists: Emphasize community on-ramps (local clubs), coach-led progression, and “gradual identity” programs to surface early de-escalation opportunities before sunk costs are large. <cite id="cd3543f7-2">Because identity mediates commitment, offering low-cost identity signals first (clubs, charity rides) and then higher-cost gear can increase escalation risk; conversely, reframing nonparticipation as identity-consistent can lower it</cite>. <cite id="cd3543f7-1">Structures that reduce precariousness and workload norms may lower escalation pressures</cite>.
  - Transportation cyclists: Provide modular bundles (bike + helmet + lock + lights) with clear ROI messaging and easy returns; use postpurchase surveys to quantify time-savings and trigger personalized nudges to pause or exit if thresholds are not met. <cite id="f3989761-1">Funnel interventions at postpurchase evaluation and divestment reduce overcommitment</cite>. <cite id="11d642de-2">Cargo-bike follow-ups quantify mode shift; non-shifts suggest de-escalation or product fit issues</cite>.

- Personalization and sequence analytics: <cite id="f3989761-0">User histories reveal sequential interests (safety, durability, portability), enabling just-in-time recommendations and friction-reduction for the next step</cite>. <cite id="f3989761-1">Cross-sell paths and drop-off points can be predicted across funnel stages</cite>. For sport segments, surface social proof and community affiliation; for commuter segments, highlight quantified time/cost metrics.

- Measurement gaps and how to close: Few studies directly stratify purchase sequences by rider type within the same firm. Track cohort-level journeys (channels → browse-to-buy → add-to-cart breadth → repeat purchase funnel → churn), segmenting by bike type (road/mountain vs commuter/cargo/e-bike) and by postpurchase telemetry (commute minutes saved, ride frequency, race participation). <cite id="11d642de-0">E-bike vs bicycle user comparisons already segment by motives and usage intensity</cite>, and <cite id="f3989761-1">funnel modeling provides a blueprint for cross-segment analysis</cite>.

Title: Escalation and de-escalation of commitment to information systems projects: Insights from a project evaluation model
Snippet: Escalation of commitment is a phenomenon that refers to situations where decision makers commit additional resources to a failing course of action (Staw, 1981). Early escalation studies suggested that the escalation phenomenon represents a syndrome of decision errors, which tends to lock decision makers into a course of action (Staw, 1981). However, an alternative definition was later proposed by Bowen (1987) which suggests that escalation of commitment can also result from a dilemma caused by the interplay between the degree of commitment to a course of action and the amount of equivocality perceived in the feedback on prior investments and in expectations for the future. Escalation studies have been applied to a variety of settings. In IS projects, commitment escalation is a widely observed phenomenon, such as in the well-known Taurus project at the London Stock Exchange (Drummond, 1996), and the case of the baggage handling system at the Denver International Airport (Montealegre and Keil, 2000). The escalation literature has suggested four types of determinants of commitment, namely project, psychological, social and structural, that together can explain the escalation phenomenon in IS settings (Staw and Ross, 1987;Keil, 1995). To alleviate the impact of project escalation, Keil and Robey (1999) have suggested a de-escalation strategy as an effective way of reducing commitment to a troubled project. 

De-escalation of commitment is defined as the ''reversal of escalating commitments to failing courses of action, either through project termination or redirection'' (Keil and Robey, 1999, p. 65). To date, the IS development literature has suggested a stage-based process model of de-escalation (Montealegre and Keil, 2000). While Montealegre and KeilÕs (2000) four-phase deescalation model fits well with large-scaled IS project context and has provided useful insights on the de-escalation process, Pan (2004) suggests that an alternative explanatory model may be necessary to explain the de-escalation process in other types of IS projects.

Snippet: Escalation of commitment theory describes individuals and organizations that maintain and often increase commitment to a venture or course of action amid prolonged evidence of ambiguous or negative outcomes (Staw, 1981). Escalation research has predominantly examined circumstances in which substantial resources were invested in a course of action that did not produce the desired outcome-frequently intended to generate a financial or economic return. 4 Over time, this behavior becomes a true escalation of commitment in the decision to repeatedly persist in a course of action given the presence of ambiguous or negative outcomes. While the logical solution to an escalation scenario would be commitment reduction, researchers have long identified the interplay of four determinants-project, psychological, social, and structural-influencing persistence in a failing course of action (Staw & Ross, 1987). Given extensive investigation of escalation behavior, less research has empirically examined both theoretical and practical applications of de-escalation of commitment (Mähring, Keil, Mathiassen, & Pries-Heje, 2008). Although initially acknowledged as withdrawal or abandonment from a failing course of action (see Staw & Ross, 1987), de-escalation behavior also manifests in a reduction of commitment by considering alternative courses of action (Montealegre & Keil, 2000). Therefore, de-escalation of commitment can be defined as the process of breaking an escalation cycle by reducing or redirecting the original failing course of action. To date, research has almost exclusively focused on the factors and processes for de-escalation in a variety of field-based qualitative case studies (see Hutchinson, 2013;Hutchinson & Bouchet, 2014a, 2014b;Keil & Montealegre, 2000;Keil & Robey, 1999;Mähring et al., 2008;Montealegre & Keil, 2000). Title: Differences of Cycling Experiences and Perceptions between E-Bike and Bicycle Users in the United States
Snippet: The purpose of this paper was to study the differences of cycling experience and perception of e-bike and bicycle users, and factors influencing the e-bike purchase decisions of bicycle users. Our study builds on previous studies exploring e-bike cycling experience and perception. However, this study focused on a comparison of differences of cycling experiences and perceptions between e-bike and bicycle users in the United States, where e-bikes are a new transportation mode. The e-bike market has matured since previous studies. Purpose-built e-bikes capture a large market share, in contrast with about half of the respondents converting conventional bicycles to e-bikes in MacArthur's study in 2013, the first nationwide survey of e-bike users in North America [1]. Also, our study is the first in the U.S. to evaluate e-bike purchase intention potential using multivariate modelling approaches. While several studies have focused on the role of an e-bike to assist older people to overcome riding barriers and to use for recreational purposes, we found that Millennials and Generation X respondents have some different e-bike cycling motives, such as cycling to save time and improve the environment, rather just to keep healthy [1,14]. Several studies reveal that e-bikes have increased riding rates and distance traveled, supporting our findings [1,12,15]. 

The data was from a U.S.-based end-consumer online survey that was distributed via IBDs. A total of 806 respondents in the U.S. took the completed survey, in which 387 respondents own regular bicycles, 122 respondents only own e-bikes, and 241 respondents own both bicycles and e-bikes. E-bike and bicycle respondents have similar demographic characteristics, including education level, household income, and family structure. The cycling characteristics and behaviors of bicycle and e-bike users were also compared and analyzed. The e-bike models were predominately city/commuter (33% of EO, 31% of BE) with other commuter and on-road styles, whereas the conventional models varied, having higher numbers of more competitive styles, such as mountain and racing/road. E-bike respondents use their e-bikes more frequently than conventional bicyclists.

Title: The impact of cargo bikes on the travel patterns of women
Snippet: In mid-2015, a survey was issued to an email list of roughly 2,500 individuals who had recently made a purchase (Riggs & Schwartz, 2015). Yuba Bicycles, a leading vendor of cargo bikes in the US, provided the list through a relationship facilitated by a California-based vendor, Cambria Bicycle Outfitters. While this was a potential limitation of the study in that it focused primarily on one particular manufacturer and consisted of individuals who had chosen to purchase a cargo bike, it had a few advantages in the study of use and modal decisions: 1) they only manufacture cargo bikes that are distributed both in the US and internationally; 2) they offer numerous cargo bike platforms for buyers to choose from (e.g. rear, electric, front-loading, small); and 3) they offer a product that is more cost-effective than other manufacturers, helping address potential limitations of cost (i.e. concerns that only the affluent can afford a cargo bike). 1 While these results might vary if the general population/non-buyers were surveyed, given that the focus of this work was to explore the challenges of those who desire to cycle via cargo bike, this limitation was counterbalanced by a follow-on qualitative evaluation. 

Surveys took approximately 10 minutes to complete and explored three factors: 1) trip mode before and after the purchase of a cargo bike (e.g. auto, transit, traditional bike, cargo bike, walk, other); 2) trip type (work, school, other); and 3) individual characteristics and preferences, focusing acutely on trips involving children. Respondents were first asked a series of questions about their travel behavior before they owned a cargo bike. They were then asked about their behavior after owning the cargo bike, using the same sequence of questions. 

Roughly 300 responses were received and a subset of 173 valid responses were assessed using descriptive statistics and crosstabs to look for associations. A valid response included someone who had both responded as having owned a cargo bike and also indicated a gender of either a male or female gender. 2 For the purposes of this work, other gender classifications were not made available. The responses were assessed for the entire population, as well as by subsets like genderexploring the different changes in behavior after owning a cargo bike.

Title: Differences of Cycling Experiences and Perceptions between E-Bike and Bicycle Users in the United States
Snippet: An online survey was conducted by Bosch eBike Systems from September 2015 to October 2015. The survey was an end-consumer online survey in the United States, which was distributed via IBDs. This survey intended to explore customers' perception of e-bikes and conventional bicycles, attempted to reveal bicycle users' riding habits, and estimated the potential opportunities and barriers to e-bike purchase. The survey questions were developed following an e-bike literature review related to e-bike purchase and riding behavior [1,6,12]. This survey focused on fully assembled e-bikes (e-bike conversions from a standard bicycle were excluded). The entire survey covers four aspects of e-bike and bicycle owners, including household characteristics, cycling experiences and behavior, motives and perception for e-bike use, future e-bike expectation, and purchase interest (for conventional bicycle owners only). Respondents who owned both a bicycle and an e-bike were presented with the e-bike related questionnaire. As an incentive for participation, respondents were entered into a chance to win an e-bike. Table 1 presents an overview summary of the survey scope. The authors acknowledge the limitations of relying solely on this sub-sample, likely missing a large portion of the e-bike market, particularly those purchased online or from big-box stores. As with most survey research, our study could suffer from self-selection bias. However, we think that this sample still represents a large and growing proportion of the current and future bicycle and e-bike markets, by both volume and value. Thus, the insights gained could provide value to public and private sector decision-makers regarding future e-bike ownership and use. 

A total of 806 respondents in the U.S. completed the survey. In the survey, 56 respondents claimed that they did not have a bicycle or e-bike. Of those, 47% said that they lived in an area which is not safe to ride, or is too hilly, or that has poor bicycling infrastructure. In addition, 15% of these respondents cannot ride because of physical limitations. Also, there were 15 bicycle respondents which stated that they no longer ride their bicycle because of physical limitations and/or because the area they live in is too hilly. These 56 respondents were excluded from the following analysis. So, the final total sample is 750 respondents.

People who are valued, approved, and have athlete characteristics by society increase their self-confidence of athletes when this situation is explained to them and they feel more like athletes, which contributes to the formation of the identity of the athlete (Reifsteck, 2011). 

Athlete identity is also one of the psychological determinants of sports commitment, that is, the level at which the person identifies with the role of the athlete is directly related to the amount of one's commitment to sports. 

The term commitment is used in psychology to describe a number of factors that may explain why people maintain relationships or engage in certain activities (Eccles, Harold, 1991). Commitment has been understood as a psychological tendency that represents a desire' and a decision to continue participating in sports' (Hassell, Sabiston & Bloom, 2010). Previous research in the field of sports psychology shows that "commitment to sports is related to participation and permanence in sports" and is defined as "a general psychological condition that represents the desire and determination to continue participating in a particular athletic program, a particular sport or sport" (Hagiwara & Isogai, 2014). Engagement is an integral part of sports participation, as athletes need to desire to learn and feel connected to their sport to continue to be part of the team. 

To bring out commitment, athletes need to enjoy what they are doing and also make a personal investment in the sport in terms of time, finances, or effort. It is also important that in sports there is social support from others and opportunities to benefit from sports, as well as a social structure and atmosphere that creates norms within the sport, creating a sense of obligation to return. These benefits can include things like relationships with others, health and fitness benefits, and mastery of a skill (Chu & Wang, 2012). 

Studies examining the relationship between athletes' athlete identity and level of commitment to sports are quite limited in the literature. Studies are mostly focused on students and young athletes. Thus, the appeal of larger communities rests on the stock of compelling narratives they have at their disposal and the capacity of these narratives to influence the moral identity of individuals. Abstract and overriding principles, then, work when they align with a compelling narrative or web-of-narratives that people draw upon to identify themselves as members of a community. For example, one is committed to principles of justice and equality because one finds the narratives offered by societies embodying these values attractive and identifies oneself in some sense as, say, a Scandinavian. 

On this reading, athletes commit themselves to principles of fair play because they find the narratives offered by, for instance, the Olympic movement or professional road cycling attractive, and identify themselves accordingly as Olympic athletes or professional road cyclists. On the conception I propose, the development of an athlete moral identity starts in the closely-knit communities of trust in which athletes live and share their sporting experiences: clubs, teams, training groups, and athlete-coach relationships. In an early stage of the development of a moral athlete identity, loyalty to these smaller communities' uniting purposes of performances, teamwork, and results appears as 'what comes naturally' to the athlete. In this stage, athletes might identify themselves as (some haphazardly chosen examples follow) 'George, the US Postal Team cyclist' or 'Alexander, the Russian crosscountry skier'. Moral development progresses as athletes expand their loyalties to direct competitors, other practitioners of the sport, and ultimately to the larger, international or even global sporting communities such as professional road cycling or the Olympic movement. Like Rorty's larger groups, the sporting communities coordinate through the creation and enforcement of abstract principles designed to balance potentially conflicting beliefs and purposes among their constituencies.

Thus, the appeal of larger communities rests on the stock of compelling narratives they have at their disposal and the capacity of these narratives to influence the moral identity of individuals. Abstract and overriding principles, then, work when they align with a compelling narrative or web-of-narratives that people draw upon to identify themselves as members of a community. For example, one is committed to principles of justice and equality because one finds the narratives offered by societies embodying these values attractive and identifies oneself in some sense as, say, a Scandinavian. 

On this reading, athletes commit themselves to principles of fair play because they find the narratives offered by, for instance, the Olympic movement or professional road cycling attractive, and identify themselves accordingly as Olympic athletes or professional road cyclists. On the conception I propose, the development of an athlete moral identity starts in the closely-knit communities of trust in which athletes live and share their sporting experiences: clubs, teams, training groups, and athlete-coach relationships. In an early stage of the development of a moral athlete identity, loyalty to these smaller communities' uniting purposes of performances, teamwork, and results appears as 'what comes naturally' to the athlete. In this stage, athletes might identify themselves as (some haphazardly chosen examples follow) 'George, the US Postal Team cyclist' or 'Alexander, the Russian crosscountry skier'. Moral development progresses as athletes expand their loyalties to direct competitors, other practitioners of the sport, and ultimately to the larger, international or even global sporting communities such as professional road cycling or the Olympic movement. Like Rorty's larger groups, the sporting communities coordinate through the creation and enforcement of abstract principles designed to balance potentially conflicting beliefs and purposes among their constituencies.

documents.snippet:
According to the perceptions of people, athlete identity plays a social role. People who are valued, approved, and have athlete characteristics by society increase their self-confidence of athletes when this situation is explained to them and they feel more like athletes, which contributes to the formation of the identity of the athlete (Reifsteck, 2011). 

Athlete identity is also one of the psychological determinants of sports commitment, that is, the level at which the person identifies with the role of the athlete is directly related to the amount of one's commitment to sports. 

The term commitment is used in psychology to describe a number of factors that may explain why people maintain relationships or engage in certain activities (Eccles, Harold, 1991). Commitment has been understood as a psychological tendency that represents a desire' and a decision to continue participating in sports' (Hassell, Sabiston & Bloom, 2010). Previous research in the field of sports psychology shows that "commitment to sports is related to participation and permanence in sports" and is defined as "a general psychological condition that represents the desire and determination to continue participating in a particular athletic program, a particular sport or sport" (Hagiwara & Isogai, 2014). Engagement is an integral part of sports participation, as athletes need to desire to learn and feel connected to their sport to continue to be part of the team. 

To bring out commitment, athletes need to enjoy what they are doing and also make a personal investment in the sport in terms of time, finances, or effort. It is also important that in sports there is social support from others and opportunities to benefit from sports, as well as a social structure and atmosphere that creates norms within the sport, creating a sense of obligation to return. These benefits can include things like relationships with others, health and fitness benefits, and mastery of a skill (Chu & Wang, 2012). 

Studies examining the relationship between athletes' athlete identity and level of commitment to sports are quite limited in the literature. Studies are mostly focused on students and young athletes. Martin et al. examined how the social identities of young athletes who were students had an impact on their commitment to sport and effort. It has been reported that commitment and effort are important in identifying the athlete with a group in the individual and group analysis (Martin et al., 2018).

documents.title: ‘Fair Play’ as a Larger Loyalty: The Case of Anti-Doping
documents.snippet:
The organisational structure of road cycling involved a majority of riders on short-term contracts with a majority of employers (i.e. teams) financially dependent on short-term sponsorships, low wages, a norm of a painstaking 80-120 racing days a year per athlete, little follow-up in training and preparation, no representative body to protect athletes' interests, and so on. Unsurprisingly, this organisational structure put many riders in a vulnerable and precarious situation and many found their loyalties not in the team or in the larger professional road cycling community, but in external networks of physicians, coaches, and other riders in similar situations. 

Surveillance and biological testing do not pull such structural issues up by the roots. Rather, as Aubel and Ohl (2014Ohl ( , 1101) ) suggest, in such a situation, wider social policy is needed 'to challenge the precariousness of the riders' careers and also that of teams'. One example of such policy can be measures that promote 'dual vocational projects (in sport and outside sport)' that increase athletes' chances of securing a rewarding job in the highly likely event that athletic results and long-term employment in sport fail to materialise (Aubel andOhl 2014, 1101). Different examples could be minimum salaries, workload restrictions and, as none are better placed than athletes to draw attention to other structural issues previously unattended to: athlete representation in policy making processes. If individualized control measures were subordinated to wider social policy, I suggest, the coordinating bodies of larger sporting communities would operate more trustworthily with the athletes' best interests in mind-that is: more inviting of their larger loyalty. 

What about the 'Anti' in Anti-doping? 

Admittedly, the loyalty redescription carries a challenge captured by the question: 'What about the "anti" in anti-doping?' This question partly arises from the elevation of the goal of creating communities of trust, common interest and interdependence above the presently overarching goal of eradicating doping.

Social cohesion (i.e., perceived opportunities for positive social interactions and friendships on a team) is related to positive emotional, motivational, and behavioral outcomes that reinforce intentions to remain on a team (8,9,11,48,54). Social cohesion also predicts higher attendance in adult recreational team sport leagues, which is possibly a behavioral manifestation of commitment (11). Among adolescent team sport participants, social cohesion is positively correlated with commitment to a team (26). 

Moreover, individuals are motivated to invest time and effort into activities that reinforce a positive sense of self (49). Therefore, athletic identity (AI), a multi-dimensional sense of self rooted in maintaining a fit/athletic appearance and being physically active, should reinforce on-going commitment to sport and PA (2). Empirical support for the inclusion of AI as a predictor of sport commitment comes from studies reporting positive correlations between AI and several SCM constructs, including enjoyment, investments, involvement opportunities, and commitment (5,20,24). Some researchers have interpreted these correlational findings to suggest that athletes who identify more strongly with the athletic role are thus more committed to their respective sport (20,24). Hagiwara and Isogai supported this proposal using a structural equation modeling approach that found Japanese college athletes' AI was a psychosocial determinant of commitment, and commitment in turn was related to their sport participation and persistency (21). Thus, our first proposed model examined athletic identity as a predictor of commitment. 

Finally, a positive relationship between psychological commitment (i.e., intentions) and behavioral commitment (i.e., participatory behaviors) has been found among adult sport and exercise participants (12,18,63).

More importantly, the present findings explain how geographic identification influences consumers" self-conceptualization and connection to the athlete. Heere and James (2007) highlighted geographic identity as one of the factors that has an impact on team identity. With respect to athlete branding, the current participants" views provide further insight into how external identities (e.g., city) can strengthen the bond between the athlete and his followers. 

Past literature argued that sport celebrities and teams can embody the local community and elevate the status of its population (see Ramshaw & Gammon, 2005;Rojek, 2006). The participants recognized the athlete and his loyalties with the city as a source of pride that served as elements capable of influencing self-assuredness, creativity, and altruistic values (Bagozzi, Gopinath, & Nyer, 1999;Verbeke, Belshcak, Bagozzi, 2004). This finding also confirms the arguments that celebrity athletes are "cosmopolitan flexible accumulators who exchange bond of city, region, and even nation" (Rojek, 2006, p. 684). Drawing conclusions about the current findings, it is clear that the athlete elevated the city"s reputation and solidified his association as a pillar of the community. 

The participants" opinions regarding the athlete"s community engagement initiatives are especially important in the light of the impact of athletes" and organizations" social responsibility actions (Babiak & Wolfe, 2009;Walker & Kent, 2009). Babiak and Wolfe (2009) have argued that "athletes promoting, for example, healthful living, may generate a larger, more attentive audience than would employees in other fields" (p. 722). Previous research confirms that various social initiatives implemented by sport organizations can enhance the overall image, add value to their brand, and influence donor commitment (Walker & Kent, 2009). In response to the questions regarding the athlete brand relationship, the participants said that the athlete made social consciousness and community engagement his top priority.
